newsitem.title: USA: Early US corn yields mixed, harvest progress slow.
newsitem.headline: Early US corn yields mixed, harvest progress slow.

text.p: Corn harvesting in key growing areas of the U.S. Midwest is unlikely to gather much momentum for a couple of weeks with farmers currently concentrating on soybeans, grain industry sources and agronomists said.
Early indications on yields have been very variable with much depending on the progress of late planted crops.
"I think by the time we get the harvest done we will be below an average yield but it is going to be better than we anticipated," Paul Bates of Bates Commodities in Normal, Illinois said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has reported that, as of Sunday, the U.S. corn harvest was nine percent complete, below the five-year average of 17 percent.
Key states such as Iowa, Illinois and Indiana are only three, six and five percent complete respectively.
"Early yields are tremendously erratic and we are probably looking at the best yields we are going to have," Bates said, noting late planting may reduce yields for some corn.
However, Bob Nielsen, extension agronomist at Purdue University in Indiana, said late planted corn may still produce reasonable yields.
"There are going to be some acceptable yields on this late planted stuff if indeed they get it mature before frost. A lot of that corn technically has looked good all summer," he said.
Nielsen said early harvesting in Indiana has mostly centered in the southwest and yields have been erratic.
"What little feedback I'm getting is that there is a little bit of everything out there. There are some very good yields, there are some very poor yields and everything in between," he said.
In Iowa, the leading corn producing state, early reports on yields were also very mixed.

"I had a report of three fields in southwest Iowa (with yields) over 200 bushels per acre. I'm afraid that's probably an isolated incident," said Dale Farnham, Iowa State University extension agronomist.

Ron Gates, grain division manager for Heart of Iowa Co-op based in Roland, Iowa, said he expected yields in his area to average around 145 to 150 bushels an acre, compared with about 150 to 155 bushels a year ago.
But corn harvest is barely underway, he added.
"When we get done with the beans in a couple of weeks I think the corn will be ready to go," he said.
